items.name: Strawberry Jam
items.summary: A classic, pectin-set strawberry jam with bright flavor and firm set. One of the best introductions to water bath canning.

steps.instruction: Prepare canner: fill water bath canner halfway with water and bring to a simmer. Wash jars and keep hot until ready to fill. Prepare new lids per manufacturer instructions.
tips: Keep jars submerged in hot (not boiling) water to prevent thermal shock when filling.

steps.instruction: Hull and crush strawberries one layer at a time with a potato masher. Measure exactly 5 cups of crushed berries into a large heavy-bottomed pot.
tips: Do not purée — small pieces of fruit give the best texture.
Slightly underripe berries contain more natural pectin.

steps.instruction: Stir powdered pectin and lemon juice into the crushed berries. Bring mixture to a full rolling boil over high heat, stirring constantly.
tips: A full rolling boil cannot be stirred down — that is your cue to add sugar.

steps.instruction: Add all the sugar at once and stir to dissolve. Return to a full rolling boil and boil hard for exactly 1 minute, stirring constantly.
tips: Set a timer for 1 minute — boiling too long degrades pectin and darkens the jam.

steps.instruction: Remove from heat. Skim foam with a metal spoon.
tips: A small pat of butter stirred in before boiling reduces foam significantly.

steps.instruction: Ladle hot jam into hot jars leaving ¼-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles with a thin spatula. Wipe jar rims with a damp cloth. Center lids and apply bands fingertip-tight.
tips: Consistent ¼-inch headspace is critical for proper sealing.

steps.instruction: Process in boiling water bath canner for 10 minutes (adjusting for altitude). Turn off heat, remove lid, and let jars stand in canner for 5 minutes.
tips: Start timing once the water returns to a full boil after adding jars.

steps.instruction: Remove jars and let cool undisturbed for 12–24 hours. Check seals: lids should not flex up and down. Refrigerate any unsealed jars and use within 3 weeks.
tips: Do not press down on lids while cooling — you may mistake the seal sound for a proper seal.

items.safety_notes: Use only tested recipes and measured ingredients. Do not reduce sugar — it is a preservative and affects the gel. Altitude above 1,000 ft requires extended processing time.
items.source: Ball Complete Book of Home Preserving

items.name: Dill Pickle Spears
items.summary: Crisp, garlicky dill pickle spears with a classic brine. Requires fresh-pack processing — no fermentation needed.

ingredients.name: Pickling or canning salt (not table salt)
Fresh dill heads or dill seed

steps.instruction: Wash cucumbers thoroughly and scrub with a vegetable brush. Remove blossom ends (opposite from stem) — blossom-end enzymes cause softening. Cut into spears or leave whole.
tips: Remove at least 1/16 inch from the blossom end.
Use cucumbers within 24 hours of picking for best crunch.

steps.instruction: Combine vinegar, water, and salt in a large saucepan and bring to a boil, stirring until salt dissolves. Keep brine hot.
tips: Use only 5% acidity vinegar. Do not alter the vinegar-to-water ratio — acidity is a safety requirement.

steps.instruction: Pack cucumber spears vertically into hot jars. Add 2 garlic cloves and 1–2 dill heads per jar. Pack tightly but without crushing.
tips: Stand spears upright for a more attractive pack.

steps.instruction: Ladle hot brine over cucumbers leaving ½-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Wipe rims, center lids, apply bands fingertip-tight.
Process in boiling water bath canner: pints 10 minutes, quarts 15 minutes. Adjust for altitude.
tips: Processing quarts any shorter risks under-sterilization.

steps.instruction: Remove jars. Let stand undisturbed 12–24 hours. Allow pickles to rest 4–6 weeks before opening for full flavor development.
tips: Pickles continue to soften if processed too long — do not extend processing time.

items.safety_notes: Never reduce vinegar, water, or salt ratios — the brine acidity keeps pickles safe. Use only standard 5% acidity vinegar. Iodized table salt causes cloudy brine and off-flavors.

items.name: Tomato Salsa
items.summary: A chunky, medium-heat salsa suited for water bath canning. The tested vinegar-to-tomato ratio ensures safe acidity.

ingredients.name: Long green chiles, seeded and chopped

steps.instruction: Peel tomatoes: score an X on the bottom, blanch 30–60 seconds in boiling water, transfer to ice bath, then slip off skins. Core and chop. Drain in a colander for 30 minutes to remove excess liquid.
tips: Draining is important — too much liquid makes a watery salsa.

steps.instruction: Roast or boil chiles and jalapeños until softened. Peel if roasted, seed, and chop finely. Measure after chopping.
tips: Wear gloves when handling hot peppers — capsaicin is persistent.

steps.instruction: Combine all ingredients in a large stainless steel saucepan. Bring to a boil over medium-high heat, stirring frequently. Reduce heat and simmer 10 minutes.
tips: Stir frequently to prevent scorching on the bottom.

steps.instruction: Ladle hot salsa into hot pint jars leaving ½-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Wipe rims, center lids, apply bands fingertip-tight.
Process in boiling water bath canner for 15 minutes. Adjust for altitude. Remove and cool undisturbed 12–24 hours.

items.safety_notes: Do not alter the proportion of low-acid vegetables (tomatoes, peppers, onions) to vinegar. Increasing low-acid ingredients without increasing vinegar lowers acidity below safe levels. Use only tested salsa recipes for canning.

items.name: Apple Butter
items.summary: Slow-cooked, spiced apple butter with a deep caramel color and spreadable texture. Uses a slow cooker for most of the cook time.

ingredients.name: Apples (tart variety), peeled, cored, and quartered

steps.instruction: Combine apples and vinegar in a large slow cooker. Cook on low 8–10 hours, stirring occasionally, until apples are completely soft.
tips: Tart apples like Granny Smith, Cortland, or Jonathan give the best flavor.

steps.instruction: Blend with an immersion blender until smooth. Stir in both sugars, spices, and lemon juice.
Return to slow cooker uncovered and cook on high 1–2 hours, stirring frequently, until mixture is very thick. A spoonful on a cold plate should not weep liquid around the edges.
tips: Leave slow cooker lid propped open a crack to allow steam to escape and concentrate the butter.

steps.instruction: Ladle hot apple butter into hot half-pint jars leaving ¼-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Wipe rims, center lids, apply bands fingertip-tight.
Process in boiling water bath canner for 15 minutes. Adjust for altitude. Remove and cool 12–24 hours.

items.safety_notes: The apple butter must be thick before canning — watery apple butter can harbor unsafe conditions in the center of the jar even after processing.
items.source: Ball Complete Book of Home Preserving

items.name: Peach Preserves
items.summary: Chunky, lightly spiced peach preserves with whole fruit pieces in a thick syrup. Excellent on biscuits or swirled into yogurt.

ingredients.name: Ripe peaches, peeled, pitted, and chopped

steps.instruction: Blanch peaches 30–60 seconds, transfer to ice bath, and slip off skins. Pit and chop into ½-inch pieces. Measure exactly 4 cups.
tips: Slightly firm peaches hold their shape better than very ripe ones.

steps.instruction: Combine peaches, lemon juice, pectin, and optional spices in a large heavy saucepan. Stir well. Bring to a full rolling boil over high heat.
Add all sugar at once. Return to a full rolling boil and boil hard for 1 minute, stirring constantly.
Skim foam. Ladle into hot half-pint jars leaving ¼-inch headspace. Remove bubbles, wipe rims, apply lids fingertip-tight.
Process in boiling water bath canner for 10 minutes. Adjust for altitude. Cool 12–24 hours.
tips: Gel set continues to firm up over 24–48 hours after processing.

items.safety_notes: Peaches are a borderline-acid fruit. Always add bottled lemon juice as specified — do not substitute fresh lemon juice as its acidity is not standardized.
items.source: Ball Complete Book of Home Preserving

items.name: Green Beans (Plain)
items.summary: Plain pressure-canned green beans — a pantry staple. The only safe method for low-acid vegetables. Raw pack is simpler; hot pack gives a tighter fill.

ingredients.name: Fresh green beans, washed and trimmed
Canning salt (optional)
ingredients.quantity: 1 tsp per quart, ½ tsp per pint

steps.instruction: Wash beans thoroughly. Snap off stem and blossom ends. Break or cut into 1–2-inch pieces.
tips: Use fresh, firm beans picked within 6–12 hours for best texture.

steps.instruction: Pack raw beans tightly into hot quart jars leaving 1-inch headspace. Add salt if desired. Pour boiling water over beans leaving 1-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles.
tips: Pack very tightly — beans shrink during processing.

steps.instruction: Wipe jar rims. Center lids. Apply bands fingertip-tight. Load jars into pressure canner with 2–3 inches of hot water in canner bottom.
Lock canner lid. Heat over high heat. Vent steam steadily for 10 minutes to purge air from the canner, then close petcock or put on weighted gauge.
tips: Incomplete venting leaves air pockets that lower internal temperature and compromise safety.

steps.instruction: Bring to pressure: 10 lb weighted gauge (or 11 lb dial gauge) at sea level. Process quarts 25 minutes, pints 20 minutes. Adjust pressure for altitude.
tips: Maintain steady pressure — fluctuating pressure stresses jars and affects safety.

steps.instruction: Turn off heat. Let canner depressurize naturally until pressure gauge reads zero. Wait an additional 10 minutes. Remove weight or open petcock. Wait 10 more minutes before opening lid.
tips: Never force cool the canner or run it under cold water — sudden depressurization causes siphoning.

steps.instruction: Remove jars with lifter. Cool undisturbed 12–24 hours on a dry towel. Check seals. Store sealed jars in a cool, dark place up to 1 year.

items.safety_notes: Green beans are a low-acid vegetable and MUST be pressure canned — water bath canning is unsafe and can result in botulism. Never reduce processing time or pressure. Discard any jar with an off odor, spurting liquid, or swollen lid without tasting.

items.name: Chicken Stock
items.summary: Rich, gelatinous chicken stock pressure-canned for long-term storage. Far superior to store-bought and shelf-stable for up to a year.

ingredients.name: Chicken carcasses, backs, or a whole stewing hen

steps.instruction: Place chicken pieces in a large stockpot. Cover with cold water by 2 inches. Bring slowly to a boil, skimming gray foam frequently for the first 20 minutes.
tips: Starting in cold water extracts more gelatin and gives clearer stock.

steps.instruction: Add all vegetables, herbs, and peppercorns. Reduce heat to a bare simmer (small bubbles only). Cook 3–4 hours.
tips: Do not boil hard — it clouds the stock and makes it fatty.

steps.instruction: Strain stock through a fine-mesh strainer. Discard solids. Defat the stock: chill overnight and lift off solidified fat, or use a fat separator immediately.
tips: Removing fat is important for clarity and flavor; fat can also impede lid sealing.

steps.instruction: Reheat strained stock to boiling. Ladle hot stock into hot quart jars leaving 1-inch headspace. Add salt if desired. Wipe rims, apply lids fingertip-tight.
Process in pressure canner at 10 lb weighted gauge (11 lb dial gauge): quarts 25 minutes, pints 20 minutes. Follow full venting and depressurization procedure.
Cool 12–24 hours. Check seals. Stock will gel solid in jars — this is normal and indicates good gelatin content.
tips: Label jars with contents and date — stock looks similar to other liquids.

items.safety_notes: Stock is a low-acid food and must be pressure canned. Do not add pasta, rice, thickeners, or flour — they alter heat penetration. These additions are safe only when added to stock after opening.

items.name: Beef Vegetable Stew
items.summary: A hearty, chunky beef and vegetable stew pressure-canned for shelf-stable meals ready to heat and eat. Do not thicken before canning.

ingredients.name: Beef chuck, trimmed and cut into 1-inch cubes

steps.instruction: Brown beef cubes in batches in a hot skillet with a small amount of oil. Season with salt and pepper. Do not cook through — just brown the exterior.
tips: Browning adds flavor through Maillard reaction — do not skip this step.

steps.instruction: Combine browned beef, vegetables, stock, tomato paste, and Worcestershire in a large pot. Bring to a boil. Simmer 15 minutes — vegetables should still be firm.
tips: Vegetables will continue cooking during processing; slightly undercooked now is correct.

steps.instruction: Ladle hot stew into hot quart jars, distributing solids and liquid evenly, leaving 1-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles thoroughly. Wipe rims, apply lids fingertip-tight.
tips: Use a wide-mouth funnel and ladle; quart jars fill more easily than pints for chunky stews.

steps.instruction: Process in pressure canner at 10 lb weighted gauge (11 lb dial gauge): quarts 90 minutes. Vent 10 minutes before closing, maintain steady pressure throughout.
Allow natural depressurization. Remove jars. Cool 12–24 hours. Check seals.
tips: A 90-minute process is long — check that canner water level is adequate at start.

items.safety_notes: Do not add flour, cornstarch, or any thickener before canning — thickeners insulate the stew interior and prevent safe heat penetration. Thicken after opening if desired. Potatoes may discolor slightly — this is safe. Discard any jar with off odors.

items.name: Classic Sauerkraut
items.summary: Traditional lacto-fermented sauerkraut made from just cabbage and salt. Requires no special equipment beyond a jar, and no heat processing if refrigerated.

steps.instruction: Remove and reserve a few outer cabbage leaves. Quarter cabbage, remove core, and slice thinly — about ⅛ inch thick. A mandoline is helpful for uniformity.
tips: Thinner shreds ferment faster and produce a more tender kraut.

steps.instruction: Combine shredded cabbage and salt in a large bowl. Toss well. Massage vigorously with clean hands for 5–10 minutes until the cabbage wilts and releases a significant amount of brine.
tips: The cabbage should look watery and feel limp — if it doesn't, wait 10 minutes and try again.
Taste the brine — it should be pleasantly salty but not overwhelming.

steps.instruction: Pack cabbage tightly into a clean quart mason jar, pushing down firmly after each handful so brine rises above the cabbage. The brine should cover the cabbage completely by at least ½ inch.
tips: Use your fist or a wooden dowel to tamp cabbage down firmly.

steps.instruction: Fold a reserved outer leaf and press it over the top of the shredded cabbage as a weight. Close jar loosely with a lid (do not seal airtight — CO₂ must escape). Alternatively, use a zip-lock bag filled with brine as a weight.
tips: The cabbage must stay submerged — exposure to air causes undesirable mold.

steps.instruction: Store at room temperature (65–75°F / 18–24°C) away from direct sunlight. Check daily. Press cabbage back under brine if it floats up. Burp the jar if using a sealed lid.
tips: Warmer temperatures ferment faster (7–10 days); cooler temperatures give more complex flavor (3–4 weeks).

steps.instruction: Taste starting at day 5–7. Kraut is ready when pleasantly sour and tangy to your preference. Transfer to refrigerator (keeps 6+ months cold) or water bath can for shelf stability.
tips: Personal taste determines doneness — there is no single right answer.

items.safety_notes: White surface film (kahm yeast) is harmless — skim it off. Fuzzy mold of any color means discard — do not attempt to salvage. Ensure cabbage stays submerged below brine at all times. Use non-iodized salt — iodine inhibits beneficial bacteria.

items.name: Simple Kimchi
items.summary: A straightforward napa cabbage kimchi (baechu-kimchi) with classic gochugaru, garlic, and ginger. Ferment 1–2 days for a fresh kimchi or longer for deep sour flavor.

ingredients.name: Fish sauce or soy sauce (for vegan)

steps.instruction: Quarter cabbage lengthwise, then cut crosswise into 2-inch pieces. Toss with salt in a large bowl. Let sit 1–2 hours, tossing every 30 minutes, until cabbage is significantly wilted and has released liquid.
tips: The cabbage should be pliable and reduced to about half its original volume.

steps.instruction: Rinse cabbage 2–3 times with cold water. Taste — it should be mildly salty. Drain and squeeze out excess water with your hands. Set aside.
tips: Thorough rinsing controls final saltiness.

steps.instruction: Mix gochugaru, garlic, ginger, fish sauce, and sugar together into a paste. Adjust gochugaru to desired heat level.
tips: Wear gloves — gochugaru stains and the capsaicin can linger on skin.

steps.instruction: Combine drained cabbage, paste, and green onions. Toss with gloved hands until every piece is coated with the red paste.
Pack tightly into a clean quart jar, pressing down after each handful to eliminate air pockets. Brine should rise above cabbage. Leave 1-inch headspace (fermentation produces CO₂). Close loosely.
Ferment at room temperature 1–5 days. Press down twice daily. Taste at day 1–2 for fresh kimchi, or continue fermenting for stronger sour flavor. Refrigerate when desired sourness is reached.
tips: Refrigerator kimchi continues to slowly ferment and improve for weeks to months.

items.safety_notes: Kimchi is a lacto-fermented food — the lactic acid produced during fermentation is its preservative. Keep vegetables submerged in liquid. White spots are kahm yeast; fuzzy mold means discard. Refrigerate after reaching desired fermentation.

items.name: Lacto-Fermented Pickles
items.summary: Old-fashioned half-sour pickles fermented in a salt brine — no vinegar, no canning. Crisp, lightly sour, and probiotic. Ready in 3–7 days.

ingredients.name: Non-chlorinated water (filtered or left out overnight)

steps.instruction: Dissolve salt in water. Stir well until fully dissolved. Set aside.
tips: Use filtered or boiled-and-cooled water — chlorine inhibits lacto-fermentation.

steps.instruction: Wash cucumbers. Remove blossom ends (at least 1/16 inch). Leave whole, halve lengthwise, or leave as spears.
tips: The blossom end contains enzymes that cause softening — always remove it.

steps.instruction: Place dill, garlic, peppercorns, grape leaves, and mustard seeds in the bottom of a clean quart mason jar. Pack cucumbers in vertically as tightly as possible without crushing.
tips: Tight packing helps keep cucumbers submerged.

steps.instruction: Pour brine over cucumbers to cover completely. Weigh down with a small zip-lock bag filled with extra brine, a small jar lid, or a fermentation weight. Seal loosely to allow CO₂ to escape.
tips: Every surface of cucumber must stay below brine.

steps.instruction: Ferment at room temperature (65–75°F) away from sunlight. Brine will become cloudy and bubbly — this is normal and a sign of active fermentation.
Taste starting at day 3. Ferment to your desired level of sourness (3 days = mild, 7 days = half-sour, 14+ days = full-sour). Refrigerate when done — fermentation nearly stops when cold.
tips: Cold storage maintains crunch significantly better than room temperature.

items.safety_notes: Keep all vegetable surfaces submerged in brine at all times. White film on the surface (kahm yeast) is harmless but should be skimmed. Discard if you see fuzzy mold. These pickles are not shelf-stable — store in refrigerator.

items.name: Sourdough Starter
items.summary: A wild-yeast sourdough starter from scratch using only flour and water. Once established, maintain indefinitely. Requires 7–14 days of daily feeding.

ingredients.name: Whole wheat or rye flour (for establishing)
ingredients.quantity: 50 g per day for first 3–5 days

steps.instruction: Day 1: Mix 50 g whole wheat flour and 50 g room-temperature water in a clean 1-quart jar. Stir vigorously to incorporate air. Cover loosely with a cloth or loose lid. Mark the level with a rubber band. Leave at 70–75°F.
tips: Using weight (grams) is more reliable than volume for flour hydration.

steps.instruction: Days 2–3: Discard all but 50 g of starter. Feed with 50 g flour and 50 g water. Stir well. Cover and return to warm spot. You may see some bubbles by day 2–3 — this is promising.
tips: The discard is important — without discarding you accumulate too much acid and the starter becomes sluggish.

steps.instruction: Days 4–7: Switch to all-purpose flour. Continue daily discard-and-feed routine. By days 5–7 the starter should be reliably doubling in volume within 4–8 hours of feeding.
tips: Starter is ready when it reliably doubles, smells pleasantly yeasty/tangy, and passes the float test (a small spoonful floats in water).

steps.instruction: Maintenance (once established): Keep at room temperature and feed daily. Or refrigerate and feed once a week. To use from fridge: pull out, feed, wait for peak activity (doubled, domed top), then use.
tips: A refrigerated starter kept for months can always be revived with a few daily feedings.

items.safety_notes: Wild fermentation can produce some odd smells in the first few days — hooch (gray liquid) on top is just alcohol from hungry yeast; stir it in or pour it off. A pink or orange streak signals contamination — discard and start over.

items.name: Strawberry Fruit Leather
items.summary: Pure strawberry fruit leather made from fresh or frozen berries — no added sugar required. Chewy, portable, and shelf-stable for months.

steps.instruction: Purée strawberries, lemon juice, and optional sweetener in a blender until completely smooth. Taste and adjust sweetness.
tips: Lemon juice brightens flavor and helps preserve color.

steps.instruction: Line dehydrator trays or rimmed baking sheets with non-stick dehydrator sheets, parchment, or plastic wrap sprayed with cooking spray.
tips: Do not use wax paper — the leather will stick and tear.

steps.instruction: Pour purée onto prepared sheets about ¼ inch thick. Tilt to spread evenly. Spread slightly thicker at edges (edges dry faster).
Dehydrate at 135°F (57°C) for 6–10 hours, or in oven at lowest setting (150–170°F) for 4–6 hours with door slightly ajar.
tips: Leather is done when it is no longer sticky to the touch in the center and peels away cleanly.

steps.instruction: While still slightly warm, peel leather off sheet and roll in plastic wrap or parchment. Store in airtight container at room temperature up to 1 month, or freeze up to 1 year.
tips: Do not store in a sealed container until completely cool to prevent moisture accumulation.

items.safety_notes: Underdried leather can mold — err on the side of slightly longer drying time. Center of the sheet should be leathery, not wet or glossy.

items.name: Beef Jerky
items.summary: Marinated, oven- or dehydrator-dried beef jerky. Pre-heating meat before dehydrating ensures pathogen safety as recommended by USDA.

ingredients.name: Beef (eye of round, flank, or top round), well-trimmed

steps.instruction: Freeze beef 1–2 hours until firm but not solid. Slice with the grain into ¼-inch strips for chewy jerky, or against the grain for tender jerky.
tips: Partially frozen meat slices far more evenly than fresh.

steps.instruction: Combine all marinade ingredients in a zip-lock bag or bowl. Add beef strips. Marinate in refrigerator 12–24 hours, turning occasionally.
tips: Longer marinating = deeper flavor but do not exceed 24 hours.

steps.instruction: Remove meat from marinade. Pat dry with paper towels. Spread strips in a single layer on dehydrator trays or oven racks over a foil-lined baking sheet.
tips: Strips should not overlap or touch — air circulation is essential.

steps.instruction: USDA safety step: Place strips on a baking rack over a sheet pan in a 275°F oven for 10 minutes before transferring to dehydrator. This pre-heating step ensures meat reaches 160°F for safety.
tips: This step is critical — most dehydrators cannot reliably reach 160°F internal temperature.

steps.instruction: Dehydrate at 165°F for 4–6 hours until strips bend and crack (not snap). Check periodically — thickness varies and affects drying time.
tips: Jerky is done when it bends and begins to crack but does not break completely.

steps.instruction: Cool completely. Store in airtight containers, glass jars, or vacuum-sealed bags. Room temperature up to 2 months; refrigerator up to 6 months; freezer up to 1 year.

items.safety_notes: Raw beef must be heated to 160°F (71°C) for safety. Relying on dehydrator temperature alone is unreliable — the USDA recommends a brief oven pre-heat step (275°F for 10 minutes) before or after dehydrating. Do not skip this step.

items.name: Dried Herb Blend
items.summary: A simple technique for preserving fresh garden herbs by drying. Applicable to basil, oregano, thyme, rosemary, sage, parsley, and more.

steps.instruction: Harvest herbs in the morning after dew has dried but before afternoon heat. Pick just before or at the start of flowering — this is when essential oil content is highest.
tips: Basil, mint, and other tender herbs should be dried quickly; thick-stemmed herbs like rosemary can be air-dried.

steps.instruction: Wash gently in cool water. Shake off excess moisture. Pat dry with clean towels. Discard damaged or discolored leaves.
Dehydrator method: Spread in a single layer on trays. Dry at 95–115°F (35–46°C) for 1–4 hours until leaves crumble when rubbed between fingers. Tender herbs dry faster; woody stems take longer.
tips: Lower temperature preserves more volatile aromatics and color.

steps.instruction: Air-dry method: Bundle 4–6 stems together with twine. Hang upside-down in a warm, dry, well-ventilated location away from direct light. Ready in 1–2 weeks.
tips: Paper bags loosely tied over bundles catch falling leaves and protect from dust.

steps.instruction: Strip leaves from stems. Crumble or leave whole. Store in airtight glass jars away from light and heat. Properly dried herbs retain potency 1–3 years.
tips: Crushing releases aroma immediately — crush just before use rather than when storing for best flavor retention.

items.safety_notes: Ensure herbs are completely dry before storing — any moisture causes mold. If herbs clump together after a few days in the jar, they were not fully dry. Re-dry immediately.
